message.reasoning:
I'm checking whether the outreach message to Sanaz Yashar is actually grounded in the source claims—zaf-091 never mentions her by name, so tying this specific suggested message to her looks fabricated.

I'm seeing this pattern repeat: contacts like Tom Anthony, Nick Fisher, and Vari Kaur are being attached to claims that never mention them, even where the inference might seem plausible given their roles. Several sections—buying signals, money momentum, tools—all show this same issue of contact references being fabricated beyond what the underlying claims actually support.

The Nick Fisher sendLine feels similarly ungrounded - it's generic outreach rather than tied to a specific fact about him, which violates the actionability requirement that sendLines be grounded in the cited fact. I'm also checking that the context_only claims with outreachSafe=false, including the Nick Fisher hobby item, are correctly placed there.

Actually zaf-110 (hobby) is marked outreachSafe: true, but the writer lumped it together with zaf-160 under a false label, mislabeling a safe claim as unsafe - that's a faithfulness error, not just misplacement. Meanwhile zaf-153 (IDF background) correctly matches its outreachSafe: false status, but I notice the item also merges in zaf-058 (career history), which is actually marked safe.

Now I'm checking the rest of the context_only items for accuracy, starting with zaf-135's Cisco investment claim, which correctly shows as unsafe.

Checking the rest of the mappings — zaf-138's UNRESOLVED competitive struggles lines up with zaf-170, zaf-142's CONFIRMED Havdala departure matches zaf-171, and zaf-139's Amex investment labeled UNRESOLVED is a reasonable inference even without an explicit status field. Now I'm verifying that the structure follows the "one item per unsafe fact" instruction.

Counting all outreachSafe=false claims (zaf-135, zaf-138, zaf-139, zaf-142, zaf-153, zaf-160, zaf-169, zaf-170, zaf-171 — nine total), the writer condensed these into only six items by merging duplicates that describe the same underlying event. That's a reasonable simplification but technically deviates from a strict one-item-per-fact rule, so it's a minor structural deduction rather than a major error. I'm now moving on to check whether the buying_signals section meets its required 3-4 item count.

I'll assume sendLine is required per item across sections following the platform standard. Now I want to spot-check that the quoted claims are actually verbatim from the source material, starting with the first buying signal item.

Checking the ABM ownership quote against zaf-090 shows a close match with only a minor capitalization difference, which is acceptable. The second item's "11 open sales roles out of 27 total" matches zaf-088 correctly and doesn't need quote marks since it's paraphrased data rather than a direct quote.

The Series C funding round mention is fine as a paraphrase since it isn't wrapped in quotation marks in the body text. The alliances strategy quote matches zaf-091 well, so now I'm moving on to verify the employee count figure for numeric accuracy.

The $130.5M funding figure and revenue band both check out against their source claims, but I'm noticing the "Aug 22, 2026" date attributed to the revenue band claim actually belongs to a different field from a separate claim, so that citation may be slightly mismatched.

Beyond that, I'm flagging a bigger issue: the money_momentum item addresses Nick Fisher about funding data with no claim actually connecting him to that information, and similarly the tools section directs a message to Nick about HubSpot/Salesforce with an arbitrary contactRef. These aren't fabrications about Nick himself, but the outreach is misdirected since nothing ties him to those specific facts, which conflicts with the instruction that contactRefs should only be used for named persons actually tied to the underlying claims.

This same pattern shows up across most major sections — buying_signals, money_momentum, tools, and how_they_sell all have items where contactRefs were added without a named person in the claims, which is a widespread structural violation that should push the structure score down significantly, maybe to a 2.

On actionability, sending outreach to arbitrary contacts about facts unrelated to them (like referencing "your recent Series C" to Nick Fisher) is inappropriate and lacks personalization, especially since Nick's own contribution (the 96% LinkedIn claim) isn't even referenced — so actionability should land around 2-3.

For faithfulness, aside from the contactRef misattribution, there's one clear fabrication: an outreachSafe status mislabeled (zaf-110), which is a genuine factual error rather than just a contact mismatch.

I'm now settling on scores: faithfulness around 3 given the real status mislabeling, specificity at 4 since the content includes solid dates and numbers, actionability at 3 due to poorly grounded sendLines, clarity at 4 since the writing is generally understandable despite some wordiness, and structure at 2 given the pervasive contactRef misuse and merging violations. The overall score should land somewhere around 4-5 out of 10, reflecting the structural and status-labeling problems as the dominant issues.

The worst problem is that sendLines and contactRefs get attributed to people who aren't actually mentioned in the underlying claims, leaving the outreach ungrounded and violating instructions. The strongest item, by contrast, is the ABM buying signal correctly linked to Vari Kaur with accurate supporting quotes and dates.
